meta.title: Paper2Learn — Turning Research Papers into Beginner Tutorials at Near-Zero Cost
meta.author: Sandeep Tiwari
meta.summary: How I designed and shipped Paper2Learn: a pipeline that ingests arXiv papers one PDF at a time, splits them into typed sections without an LLM, stores them compactly in MongoDB Atlas, and turns them into beginner-friendly tutorials only when an admin asks — with copyright checks, human approval, live progress over Server-Sent Events, and a deployment that costs close to $0.

thumbnail.alt: Paper2Learn pipeline: arXiv PDF to sections to MongoDB Atlas to AI simplification to tutorial

content.tle: Paper2Learn — Turning Research Papers into Beginner Tutorials at Near-Zero Cost
content.smr: Research papers are written for experts. Paper2Learn reads new papers from arXiv, understands their structure without AI, and produces tutorials that answer what a beginner actually asks: what is it, why does it matter, how does it work, and what should I learn next? AI is used for one thing only, simplification, and a human approves every tutorial before it is published.

img.alt: Paper2Learn system architecture: sources, deterministic ingestion, MongoDB Atlas storage, FastAPI serving, and the admin-triggered AI simplification lane
img.caption: End-to-end architecture. The top row runs without any AI; the red lane runs only when an admin clicks Process.

content.p: Hundreds of AI papers appear on arXiv every day. Summaries exist, but a summary does not teach. A beginner needs the idea in plain words, the intuition behind the method, how it is implemented, what the results really mean, and which concepts to study first.
The engineering challenge was to do this reliably and cheaply: no duplicate papers, no lost data, no runaway AI bills, no copyright problems, and a deployment that fits entirely inside free tiers.
content.quote: Design rule: use deterministic code for everything deterministic, and spend AI only where language understanding is genuinely needed.

list.item: Sources — arXiv search API for papers, arXiv OAI-PMH for each paper's licence.
Ingestion — one PDF at a time: download, hash, extract, section, licence, save, delete. No AI.
Storage — MongoDB Atlas M0 (free, 512 MB) with full-text and vector search.
Serving — a FastAPI service on Render Free: REST APIs, retrieval tools, blog XML, admin console.
AI lane — only when an admin clicks Process: embeddings and a simplified tutorial, then deterministic checks and human review.
Delivery — every push is tested in GitHub Actions and deployed to Render automatically; a daily workflow ingests new papers.

content.codet:
arXiv API ──► GitHub Actions (daily) / Admin "Run now" │ one PDF at a time, never stored ▼ metadata ─► dedup(source id) ─► stream PDF ─► SHA-256 ─► dedup(hash) ─► PyMuPDF extract ─► sectioner ─► licence ─► MongoDB ─► delete temp PDF
Admin clicks "Process" (one paper) ──► Gemini: embeddings + summary/JSON ─► copyright + grounding checks ─► PENDING_REVIEW ─► human approves ─► /api/v1/blog/posts/{slug}.xml ─► sandeeptiwari.me renders it
content.hd1: 3. Ingestion: One PDF at a Time
content.p: The hosting constraints shaped the pipeline. Render Free has 512 MB of memory and no persistent disk, and Atlas M0 has 512 MB of storage. So the pipeline never keeps a PDF: each file is streamed to a temporary file, processed, and deleted before the next one starts. Only structured data reaches the database.

list.item: Fetch metadata from the arXiv API (respecting its limit of one request every three seconds).
Skip the paper if its source ID is already stored — before downloading anything.
Stream the PDF to a temp file while computing its SHA-256 hash, with a size cap, a PDF signature check and an SSRF guard that rejects private or non-HTTPS targets, including after redirects.
Skip the paper if the same content hash already exists (a second deduplication level).
Extract text with PyMuPDF. Large PDFs are split into page ranges processed in parallel worker processes, then joined in page order.
Split the paper into typed sections (next section), look up its licence, save everything, and delete the temp file.

content.p: Every step is idempotent. Re-running the same window, or importing papers that are already present, inserts nothing twice. One failing paper never stops the batch: the error is recorded and the run continues.

arXiv's edge consistently answered one HTTP client library with an empty 406 response, while byte-identical requests from Python's standard library succeeded. After ruling out headers, TLS settings and header order, the metadata client was switched to the standard library and the behaviour was documented. Verifying live behaviour, rather than trusting the documentation, saved a lot of guesswork later.

Tutorials need the right parts of a paper: the introduction for "what is it", the method for "how does it work", the results for "what did they find". Instead of asking an LLM to find them, a deterministic sectioner reads the PDF layout.

list.item: The body font size is the size carrying the most characters; headings are short lines that are bold or larger.
It recognises LaTeX-style numbered headings ("2" followed by "Related Work"), inline headings ("3 Method") and IEEE style ("III. APPROACH", "B. Sub-title").
A numbering-sequence check rejects table values such as "65.3" that happen to be styled like headings.
Keyword rules map headings to types: introduction, background, method, experiments, results, discussion, limitations, conclusion, references, appendix.
Untitled sections between the introduction and the experiments are inferred as method and marked as inferred.

content.p: On real arXiv papers, the share of papers needing human review fell from 43% to about 18% after adding IEEE support and the sequence check. The remaining papers go to a review queue instead of producing a poor tutorial.
The free Atlas cluster has about 512 MB. The target was roughly 500 papers with a healthy margin, so I measured before designing the final schema.

list.item: Before optimising: about 315 KB per paper, mostly because the full text was stored twice and the full-text index was huge.
Dropped the duplicate full text; the text is rebuilt from sections when needed.
No text stored for references, acknowledgements or front matter; appendices capped; a per-paper text cap for outliers.
Full-text index restricted to body sections through a partial index.
Embeddings stored as compact float32 binary vectors — 3 KB for 768 dimensions — with chunk text read from sections by offset, never duplicated.
Tutorial XML rendered on demand from the stored draft; traffic metrics stored as daily aggregates with automatic expiry.

content.p: Measured result on Atlas: about 230 KB per paper including indexes, so 500 papers take about 125 MB — roughly a quarter of the free cluster. The biggest lesson: a MongoDB text index cost about 3.4 times the text it indexed, much more than I had estimated, which is exactly why measuring beats guessing.
Before any AI is involved, the data is already searchable and retrievable in a controlled way.

list.item: Full-text search over paper titles, abstracts and section text, using MongoDB's built-in text index at no extra cost.
Semantic search: sections are chunked deterministically, embedded with Gemini, and queried through Atlas Vector Search.

Five retrieval tools with JSON schemas in LLM tool-calling format: search papers, get a paper outline, get the sections suggested for a learning goal, get specific sections, and search inside sections.
Every text-returning tool has a hard character budget and reports what was truncated or missing, so a model can never pull a whole paper by accident.

content.p: Learning goals map to section types: overview (abstract, introduction, conclusion), how it works (method, background), implementation (method, experiments, appendix), evaluation (experiments, results, discussion, limitations) and prerequisites (background, related work, introduction).
content.hd1: 7. AI Simplification with a Human in the Loop
content.p: Early runs showed that calling the model automatically for every new paper wasted calls and made progress hard to follow. The final design makes AI an explicit admin action.

list.item: The admin console lists pending and processed papers with counts.
The admin clicks Process on one paper; only one AI job runs at a time.
One call creates the chunk embeddings; one call produces the simplified summary and a structured tutorial as validated JSON.
Progress streams live to the browser over Server-Sent Events: embeddings, summary, completed or failed, with a percentage bar.
Deterministic checks run on the result, and the tutorial waits in PENDING_REVIEW.
A human reads it and approves or rejects it. Only approved tutorials appear on the blog.

content.p: The tutorial always follows the same beginner structure: What is it, Why does it matter, How does it work, How is it implemented, What did they find, Key concepts, What to learn next, and Source and licence. It is rendered into the same XML format as this article.

list.item: Two model calls per paper, about 5,000 input and 1,600 output tokens for the tutorial.
A finished draft is reused instead of regenerated unless a new version is explicitly requested.
Daily call caps, a minimum spacing between calls and hard HTTP timeouts, so a throttled request fails visibly instead of hanging.
Every AI result records provider, model, prompt version, sectioner version, input sections, token counts and timestamps.

content.p: Ideas and results are not protected by copyright; a paper's wording, figures and tables are. Each paper's licence is fetched from arXiv and mapped to a policy. In a sample of 107 papers, about 41% used licences that grant no reuse rights, so this mattered.

list.item: The prompt requires original wording, at most one short attributed quote, and no reproduced figures or tables.

A verbatim detector compares the tutorial with the paper using 8-word shingles and enforces per-licence limits on the longest copied run and the copied ratio. In a live run it caught a copied 16-word sentence.
A grounding check requires every number in the tutorial to appear in the paper excerpts, which guards against invented results.
Restrictive licences need an explicit licence acknowledgement and a written note before approval.
Every tutorial ends with attribution, a link to the original paper and its licence. PDFs are never stored or redistributed.

list.item: Dashboard: Atlas usage and KB per paper, per-collection data and index sizes, licence mix and tutorial status counts.
LLM token usage per day and model, and API traffic per day and per route, stored as small aggregated counters.
Paper management: add a paper by arXiv ID, search, edit metadata, delete with confirmation.
Processing: pending, processed, failed and needs-review lists with one-click processing and live progress.
Review queues for sectioning and tutorials, and a manual ingestion run with streamed events.
Render Free runs the FastAPI service with a production ASGI server, configuration from environment variables, and a health endpoint that returns UP without touching the database.
MongoDB Atlas M0 stores everything, including vector search.
GitHub Actions runs the test suite against a real MongoDB service container on every push, then triggers the Render deploy hook and checks health.
A scheduled workflow ingests new papers daily — no AI calls, so no model cost.
Gemini's free tier covers embeddings and summaries within daily caps.
An Atlas IP access-list block surfaces as a TLS handshake error, not an access error. Knowing that turned a confusing SSL failure into a one-minute fix.
Hosting dashboards can keep spaces in imported variable names, so the app now normalises names and the admin console shows which settings the server actually resolved.
A single missing parenthesis blanked the admin page, so the console's JavaScript is now syntax-checked in CI.
Free hosting sleeps when idle; long work runs in GitHub Actions or as short, resumable admin jobs.
Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn
PyMuPDF for PDF extraction and layout analysis
MongoDB Atlas with full-text search and Atlas Vector Search; PyMongo
Gemini for embeddings and structured generation
Server-Sent Events for live progress; a vanilla-JavaScript admin console
pytest with real MongoDB integration tests, headless-browser UI checks
Render, GitHub Actions, Docker Compose for local development
115 papers ingested and split into about 2,700 typed sections.
About 230 KB per paper, leaving room for roughly 1,700 papers before reaching 80% of the free cluster.
Two model calls per processed paper, with every tutorial reviewed by a human before publishing.
Next: a side-by-side review view that highlights copied runs, semantic retrieval in tutorial generation, and more sources such as OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar.

content.quote: The most valuable decisions were not about AI: measuring storage before designing the schema, keeping ingestion deterministic, and making every AI step explicit, observable and reviewable.
